titre: Wallace's Line, an Invisible Border Between Bali and Lombok
accroche: Between two Indonesian islands just 35 km apart, the fauna switches from an Asian world to an Australian one.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1856, the British naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace crosses in two hours the strait separating Bali from Lombok, two Indonesian islands barely thirty-five kilometers apart. On the first, he collects barbets, bulbuls, and woodpeckers; on reaching the second, these birds vanish all at once, replaced by cockatoos, honeyeaters, and megapodes that he has met nowhere farther west in the archipelago. Nothing in the landscape, the climate, or the vegetation prepares you for this switch. Two hours at sea, and an entire continent of animal life changes.

## The Mechanism

Wallace formalizes the observation in 1860, in a paper published by the Linnean Society of London under the title “On the Zoological Geography of the Malay Archipelago”: a line, invisible at the surface, divides the Malay Archipelago into two zoological worlds. In the west, an Asian fauna (tigers, elephants, rhinoceroses, monkeys); in the east, a fauna related to Australia's (marsupials, cockatoos, and, farther off in New Guinea, monotremes). The line runs between Borneo and Sulawesi, then between Bali and Lombok, exactly where Wallace had made his observation.

The cause cannot be seen from a boat: it lies underwater. To the west of the line, Borneo, Sumatra, Java, and Bali rest on the Sunda Shelf, a submerged platform less than two hundred meters deep that extends Southeast Asia. During the Pleistocene glaciations, when sea level dropped by as much as one hundred twenty meters, this shelf was almost entirely exposed: a continuous land bridge then linked the Asian continent to Bali, allowing land mammals to cross on foot. To the east, Australia and New Guinea sit on a symmetrical shelf, the Sahul Shelf. But between the two shelves, the Lombok Strait, at the very spot where Wallace made his observation, reaches a depth of at least 250 meters, and the Makassar Strait, farther north, is likewise a deep-water channel that cleanly separates the two shelves: two barriers that no drop in sea level, even at its glacial minimum, one hundred twenty meters at most, ever allowed anyone to cross dry-shod.

## The Shift

The most natural intuition would have it that two islands thirty-five kilometers apart share, more or less, the same fauna: proximity, we assume, makes kinship. Wallace's line reverses this reasoning. It is not surface distance that decided the kinship of species, but an invisible topography, that of the ocean floor, which has stayed the same for millions of years whatever the sea level at any given moment. Two nearby islands can thus belong to two entirely separate biological histories, while lands much farther apart on either side of the same continental shelf share the same fauna.

The border has withstood time better than its purely geographic nature would suggest. A 2021 synthesis published in the journal Biological Reviews by the biogeographers Jason R. Ali and Lawrence R. Heaney traces a century and a half of debate over the exact course and the name of this border: the split between Asian and Australian faunas has never been called into question, but its precise course around Sulawesi (where the Makassar Strait reproduces on a larger scale what the Lombok Strait does between Bali and Lombok) has been redrawn several times since Wallace. The name established by usage, “Wallace's line,” is, moreover, not Wallace's own, and he never adopted it: it was the biologist Thomas Henry Huxley who coined it in 1868, in homage to a border its discoverer had described without giving it a name.

citation.texte: In Bali we have barbets, fruit-thrushes, and woodpeckers; on passing over to Lombock these are seen no more, but we have abundance of cockatoos, honeysuckers, and brush-turkeys, which are equally unknown in Bali, or any island further west. [...] The strait is here fifteen miles wide, so that we may pass in two hours from one great division of the earth to another, differing as essentially in their animal life as Europe does from America.
citation.source: The Malay Archipelago (1869), chapter I (“Physical Geography”)

carte.punch: Just 35 km apart, two islands with faunas as different as Europe's and America's.
carte.idee: In 1856, Wallace notices that on crossing the 35 km strait between Bali and Lombok, the fauna changes radically. The border is not on land but underwater: the strait plunges to more than 250 m, too deep for a land bridge ever to have spanned it, even at the lowest sea levels of the glacial periods.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: A 2021 synthesis of the history of the debates over the course and name of Wallace's line, notably around Sulawesi — the authors show that the lines proposed since Wallace have remained permeable, with no definitive consensus on their course.

quiz.question: Why does the fauna change radically between Bali and Lombok, when the two islands are only 35 km apart?
choix: Because the two islands have opposite climates, one humid and tropical, the other arid
Because European breeders introduced different species on each island in the 19th century
Because the strait separating them is too deep ever to have been a land bridge, even when sea level dropped by 120 m
Because a recent volcanic eruption wiped out Lombok's Asian fauna
quiz.explication: Bali sits on the Sunda Shelf, which was exposed during the glaciations and connected to Asia; the Lombok Strait, by contrast, reaches a depth of at least 250 m and was never dry, even at the lowest sea level of the Pleistocene. Climate and volcanic eruptions explain nothing about this abrupt switch.
